title: SPATIAL AND SOCIAL ASPECTS OF CROWDING PERCEPTION
research_question: To examine the effects of room color and visual complexity on perceptions of room capacity and judgments of crowding, and how these effects are mediated by social vs. nonsocial activity orientation.

participants.description: Eighty male and female undergraduates at the State University of New York at Stony Brook. More than 80% were raised in Metropolitan New York, with similar ages and family histories.
participants.recruitment: Received partial course credit in Introductory Psychology as compensation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four scale model rooms (20.5 ft square, 8.5 ft high at 1:18 scale) made of plywood with cork floors. Two rooms were painted light green (Sears No. 0866), two dark green (Sears No. 0872). Two rooms had low visual complexity (devoid of features), and two had high visual complexity (pictures on two walls: 2.5x2.5 inch graphic lion, 2.5x2.5 inch bridge painting, 1.5x2.5 inch city street picture). Small clothespin figures (3.5 inches tall, representing 5 ft 8 inch people) were used.

measures.instrument: Number of clothespin figures placed in the model room until the subject began to feel crowded.
Location of the figure representing the subject in the model room (e.g., right half near pictures).
Background questionnaire (age, sex, SAT scores, ordinal position, family size, current home address, childhood environment type)

findings.antecedent: Room color (light green vs. dark green)
findings.consequent: Number of figures placed in the room (crowding criterion)
findings.mechanism: Light colors cause interiors to appear larger, increasing perceived available space, thus increasing the threshold for crowding.
findings.quote: color differences accounted for a significant amount of the variance in the number of figures placed in each room (F = 25.116, p < .001): more figures were placed in the light green rooms than in the dark green rooms

findings.consequent: Number of figures placed in the room (crowding criterion)
findings.quote: the visual complexity variable did not account for a significant share of the variance (F = .836, p > .3)

findings.consequent: Number of figures placed in the room (crowding criterion)
findings.quote: the effect of orientation reported by Desor was not obtained (F = .482, p > .4).

findings.antecedent: Interaction of orientation (social vs. nonsocial) and room color (light green vs. dark green) in high visual complexity rooms
findings.consequent: Number of figures placed in the room (crowding criterion)
findings.mechanism: In nonsocial settings, visual complexity in dark rooms might add to sensory overload, reducing perceived capacity. In social settings, it might provide alternative loci for attention, reducing social stimulation.
findings.quote: When the high complexity conditions were considered alone, the interaction of orientation and room color approached significance (F = 2.72, p = .1); while the number of figures placed in the light green room and the dark green room considered under social orientation was comparable, the number placed in the dark green room considered under nonsocial conditions was considerably lower.

findings.consequent: Tendency to place self in the right half near pictures
findings.mechanism: Visually complex stimuli provide additional loci of person-environment transaction, allowing individuals to attend to nonsocial elements and reduce social stimulation.
findings.quote: those considering high complexity rooms tended to place themselves in the right half near the pictures (X2 = 6.084, df = 1, p < .05).

findings.antecedent: Dark green, high visual complexity room under nonsocial orientation
findings.consequent: Self-placement in the right half near pictures
findings.mechanism: In nonsocial settings, visual complexity in dark rooms might add to sensory overload, reducing the appeal of these areas for self-placement.
findings.quote: Self-placement in the right half of the dark, high complexity room considered under nonsocial conditions was considerably lower than in the other rooms characterized by high visual complexity.

findings.antecedent: Room color (dark green vs. light green)
findings.mechanism: Light colors cause interiors to appear larger, increasing perceived available space.
findings.quote: The differences in color did influence the perceived size of the rooms, as subjects considering dark green rooms rated them significantly smaller than those rating light green rooms (F = 26.259, p < .001).

findings.antecedent: Interaction of room color, visual complexity, and orientation
findings.mechanism: The combination of dark color (limits perceived space) and additional nonsocial stimulation from visual complexity (in nonsocial settings) reduces perceived room size.
findings.quote: an interaction among the three major independent variables indicated that the dark green room characterized by high visual complexity was perceived as smaller than other high complexity rooms when considered under a nonsocial orientation (F = 15.003, p < .001).

findings.antecedent: Room color (dark green vs. light green)
findings.mechanism: Dark colors reduce perceived spatial availability, contributing to feelings of stuffiness.
findings.quote: Ratings of stuffiness (F = 15.346, p < .001) and the degree to which crowding was perceived in the rooms (F = 10.544, p < .01) were also influenced by room color

findings.antecedent: Interaction of room color, visual complexity, and orientation
findings.mechanism: The combination of dark color and additional nonsocial stimulation from visual complexity (in nonsocial settings) contributes to feelings of stuffiness.
findings.quote: showed the same three-way interactions as did ratings of room size (F = 5.389, p < .05 and F = 5.816, p < .05).

findings.antecedent: Room color (dark green vs. light green)
findings.mechanism: Dark colors reduce perceived spatial availability, lowering the threshold for crowding.
findings.quote: Ratings of stuffiness (F = 15.346, p < .001) and the degree to which crowding was perceived in the rooms (F = 10.544, p < .01) were also influenced by room color

findings.antecedent: Interaction of room color, visual complexity, and orientation
findings.mechanism: The combination of dark color and additional nonsocial stimulation from visual complexity (in nonsocial settings) increases perceived crowdedness.
findings.quote: showed the same three-way interactions as did ratings of room size (F = 5.389, p < .05 and F = 5.816, p < .05).
a significant sex effect was found for ratings of how much subjects liked the rooms: female subjects indicated that they liked the rooms more than males did (F = 7.031, p < .05).

findings.antecedent: Room color, visual complexity, or social orientation
findings.quote: The absence of any effects of room color, visual complexity, or social orientation on the ratings of prettiness and attraction indicated that these manipulations did not alter aesthetic ratings of the rooms or influence preference for them.

findings.antecedent: Personal characteristics (age, family size, ordinal position, residential history)
findings.quote: Personal characteristics, including age, family size, ordinal position, and residential history, were not related to any of the dependent variables; correlations for these relationships did not exceed .25.

mechanisms: Light colors cause interiors to appear larger, increasing the amount of space perceived as available for use, thereby increasing the threshold for crowding.
Dark colors result in perceptions of decreased spatial availability, lowering the threshold for crowding.

Visually complex stimuli provide additional loci for person-environment transaction, allowing individuals to attend to nonsocial elements and reduce unwanted social stimulation, especially in social settings.
In nonsocial settings, the combination of dark color and additional nonsocial stimulation from visual complexity can lead to sensory overload, reducing perceived room size and capacity.
moderators: Room Color (light green vs. dark green)
implementation_implications: Designers can increase comfortable room densities by varying color, specifically using light colors to increase perceived spatial extent.

It is important to consider multiple environmental elements (color, visual complexity) and their interactions, as well as the psychological characteristics of users, when making design decisions to influence perceptions of crowding and room capacity.

limitations: Generalizability is limited as subjects in model-room studies do not have real experience in the setting.
Visual properties may assume artificial importance due to the absence of other sensory cues (olfactory, tactile) present in actual experience, potentially exaggerating their impact.
The elimination of other sensations and direct interaction demands may have hindered a realistic examination of crowding as an interpersonal process.
Findings must be replicated and extended in actual settings with complete interpersonal interaction.
The sample was relatively homogeneous (mostly from Metropolitan New York), which may have limited the observation of differences along background characteristics.
The factorial design did not allow subjects to compare norms across different orientations, potentially reducing variability.
The use of model rooms may not be sufficient for studying varying criteria for crowding.

Potential confounds of orientation with normative expectations, where pictures in a room might be perceived as more suitable for a cocktail party than an airport lounge, influencing perceived suitability for social activity rather than pure complexity.

paper_metadata.title: Spatial and Social Aspects of Crowding Perception
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Spatial and Social Aspects of Crowding Perception
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This paper discusses mediation of the crowding experience in architectural interiors by three environmental variables: setting orientation, room color, and visual complexity of the interior. Subjects' perceptions of space available and thresholds of crowding were assessed by the placement of miniature figures in model rooms and room ratings along several dimensions. Data presented indicated that perceptions of physical space available in the setting and crowding thresholds are effectively mediated by variations in interior design. While the actual amount of space was kept constant, subjects perceived dark rooms as smaller and crowded with fewer figures than corresponding light rooms. High visual complexity was found to interact with setting orientation and room color; nonsocial dark rooms were perceived as smaller than other high complexity interiors. The implications of these results for the design of interior spaces are discussed.

environmental_features: room color (light green vs. dark green)
number of figures/objects in the room (density manipulation)

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Examines how objective spatial features (e.g., room color, density) influence the subjective experience and perception of crowding.
Investigates specific spatial cues as moderators of crowding perception, building on existing frameworks of person-environment interaction.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper explores how specific spatial characteristics of an environment influence an individual's perception of crowding, leading to behavioral outcomes.

steps.to_construct: behavioral responses (e.g., number of figures placed as a crowding criterion)

instruments_used.name: Crowding Criterion Task
instruments_used.description: Participants are asked to place figures or objects in a room until they feel it is crowded, providing a behavioral measure of crowding tolerance.

instruments_used.name: Self-report questionnaires
instruments_used.description: Likert-scale items or semantic differentials to assess subjective states related to the environmental conditions.
